titles.611: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR — each dies own death / own corruption; still 'die in Adam' may pertain to imputation
titles.612: Man. Post. Cap. IX: PLAC — imputation of Adam's death? unheard-of; then 'sinned in Adam' can stand without sin imputed
titles.613: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR — if 'die in Adam' looks to imputation, so does 'sinned in Adam'; only Adam, not Noah etc.
titles.614: Man. Post. Cap. IX: GAR — discrimination not mere natural propagation, nor Adam-as-origin alone

latin.611: GAR. Nec minus certum est unumquemque nostrum mori morte sua propria, & habere corruptionem internam sibi propriam, & personaliter distinctam a corruptione quam peccatum actuale fecit in Adamo. Habere autem utrumque ex vi conjunctionis illius quae nobis cum Adamo tanquam capite generis intercedit. Illa tamen non impediunt, quominus ad imputationem ea verba Apostoli pertinere dicantur, cum testatur, nos in Adamo mori.
latin.612: PLAC. Itane, ad imputationem mortis Adami? Quis unquam audiverat, mortem Adami nobis imputari? Manet igitur responsio mea, vel si ita vis, argumentatio: si propositio in Adamo morimur vera est, quamvis mors Adami nobis non imputetur, etiam propositio in Adamo peccavimus vera esse potest, quamvis peccatum Adami nobis non imputetur.
latin.613: GAR. Unde contrario modo concludo, atque collegit Vir doctus: Si dictum Apostoli, in Adamo morimur, ad imputationem spectat: Ergo & quod ait, in Adamo peccasse. Atqui illud ad imputationem spectat; ut certa ratione ostendi potest. Nam neque in Noacho, neque in quocumque alio maiorum nostrorum mori dicimur, sed tantum in Adamo. Et tamen sicuti dicimur ab Adamo prognati, ita dici possumus prognati a patribus & omnibus maioribus nostris.
latin.614: Cuius discriminis aliquam prorsus causam esse oportet. Non est autem illa simpliciter quaerenda in conjunctione naturali, aut propagatione qua descendimus ab Adamo. Nam non minus a maioribus alijs nostris propagati sumus, neque minus sumus cum iis coniuncti, quam cum Adamo; imo propinquior est cum iis, quam cum Adamo, communio ratione temporis. Neque etiam in eo, quod Adam principium est nostrae originis, sive ille a quo genus humanum incepit. Nam ea quidem legitima causa esse potest, quare in Adamo mori dicamur: sed non est legitima causa quare idem de alijs maioribus dici non possit. &c.
latin.615: PLAC. Quomodo certa ratione ostendi potest, dictum Apostoli in Adamo morimur, ad imputationem spectare, si sine imputatione causa legitima est, quare in Adamo mori dicamur? Agebatur enim de eo quod ab Apostolo dicitur, non de eo quod non dicitur. At quare idem de alijs maioribus non dicitur? Si saepius diceretur ac inculcaretur in Scriptura nos in Adamo mori, merito quaeri posset, quare saepe rem illam repetens Scriptura, perpetuo unius Adami, nunquam aliorum maiorum meminisset: nunc, cum semel dictum sit, mirum videri non debet, si alij maiores silentio praeteriti sunt, nec locus est silentii illius rationem quaerendi.
latin.616: Si tamen eius ratio reddenda est, ab imputatione arcessiri non debet: succresceret enim statim alia quaestio, cur non aeque in alijs maioribus, ac in Adamo, quod imputaretur posteris fuisset? Tandemque ad Dei voluntatem esset confugiendum, quae sine imputatione posset hoc loco pro ratione afferri. Sed non est opus: succurrunt enim aliae rationes, & quidem duae. Prima, a voce omnes. Sicut, inquit Apostolus, omnes in Adamo morimur. Iam autem manifestum est omnes in solo Adamo mori. Altera inde peti potest, quod notatur primus fons, prima origo mortis. Reliqui maiores veluti canales fuerunt, per quos peccatum & mors ab illo fonte in nos dimanarunt: solus Adamus primus fuit author mortis.

pass_a.611: Garrigues grants each dies his own death and has his own internal corruption, personally distinct from what Adam's act wrought in Adam—yet both come from union with Adam as race-head. Those personal facts, he says, still let Paul's 'we die in Adam' pertain to imputation.
pass_a.612: Placeus balks at 'imputation of Adam's death' as unheard-of. His parallel stands: if dying in Adam can be true without Adam's death imputed, sinning in Adam can be true without Adam's sin imputed.
pass_a.613: Garrigues flips Placeus's inference the other way: if 'we die in Adam' looks to imputation, then so does talk of having sinned in Adam. He starts a 'sure reason': we are never said to die in Noah or any other ancestor—only in Adam—though we are as truly descended from those fathers as from Adam.
pass_a.614: So Adam must be marked off somehow. Not by bare natural propagation—we are as joined to later ancestors, and nearer in time to them than to Adam. Not merely because Adam began the race: that may explain saying we die 'in Adam,' but it is not a legitimate cause why the same cannot also be said of other ancestors.
pass_a.615: Placeus presses the method hard: how can you prove by a sure reason that 'we die in Adam' looks to imputation, if without imputation there is already a legitimate cause for saying we die in Adam? The debate concerns what the Apostle says, not what he omits. And because Scripture says it only once, silence about other ancestors is unsurprising—frequent repetition would invite asking why only Adam is named.
pass_a.616: Tip: do not explain that silence by imputation—why then was there not something in other ancestors equally to be imputed to posterity, ending in a retreat to bare divine will without imputation? Better: two reasons come to hand. First, the word 'all'—all die in Adam alone. Second, Adam is marked as the first source and author of death; the rest were only channels from that spring. Tip before Jeroboam / omnes-peccaverunt.

611: GAR. It is no less certain that each of us dies by his own proper death, and has an internal corruption proper to himself and personally distinct from the corruption which actual sin made in Adam. Yet we have both by the force of that conjunction which joins us to Adam as head of the race. Still those facts do not keep the Apostle's words from being said to pertain to imputation when he testifies that we die in Adam.
612: PLAC. Really—to the imputation of Adam's death? Who ever heard that Adam's death is imputed to us? So my answer—or if you will, my argument—stands: if the proposition "we die in Adam" is true even though Adam's death is not imputed to us, the proposition "we sinned in Adam" can also be true even though Adam's sin is not imputed to us.
613: GAR. From which I conclude the opposite way from the learned man: if the Apostle's saying "we die in Adam" looks to imputation, then so does what he says about having sinned in Adam. And that saying does look to imputation, as can be shown by a sure reason. For we are not said to die in Noah, nor in any other of our ancestors, but only in Adam. And yet just as we are said to be descended from Adam, so we can be said to be descended from our fathers and all our ancestors.
614: There must be some cause at all of this discrimination. But it is not to be sought simply in the natural conjunction or propagation by which we descend from Adam. For we are no less propagated from our other ancestors, nor less joined to them than to Adam; indeed our communion with them is nearer in time than with Adam. Nor again simply in this, that Adam is the principle of our origin, or the one from whom the human race began. For that can indeed be a legitimate cause why we are said to die in Adam; but it is not a legitimate cause why the same cannot be said of other ancestors. Etc.
615: PLAC. How can it be shown by a sure reason that the Apostle's saying "we die in Adam" looks to imputation, if without imputation there is already a legitimate cause why we are said to die in Adam? For the point was what the Apostle says, not what he does not say. But why is the same not said of other ancestors? If Scripture said and drove home more often that we die in Adam, one might fairly ask why, repeating that matter often, it always remembered one Adam and never other ancestors; now, since it is said only once, it ought not seem strange if other ancestors are passed over in silence, and there is no place to hunt a reason for that silence.
616: Yet if a reason for it must be given, it ought not be fetched from imputation: for at once another question would grow up—why was there not equally in other ancestors, as in Adam, something to be imputed to posterity? And at last one would flee to God's will, which without imputation could be offered here as the reason. But there is no need: other reasons come to hand, and two of them. First, from the word "all." As the Apostle says, we all die in Adam. And it is already plain that all die in Adam alone. Second, it can be drawn from this, that the first source, the first origin of death, is marked. The other ancestors were like channels through which sin and death flowed down from that source into us: Adam alone was the first author of death.
